To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in 2D the scattering length and effective range exist for any potential with an asymptotic behavior V(r) ~ 1/r ^{2+ε}, ε>0, while in 3D the scattering length exists for any ε>0, but the effective range exists only for ε≥1.

the scattering length and effective range are defined in the low-energy limit for a wide class of potentials, including all potentials that decay faster than a power of the distance, but not for potentials that decay as a power of the radial coordinate.

the S-wave scattering length and the effective range of a central potential are defined for a power-law potential in two and in three dimensions, if the potential falls off faster than the inverse square root of the distance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the behavior of the phase shifts for central potentials in 2D and 3D.
the low-energy behavior of scattering in two and threedimensions.
the study of low-energy potential scattering in the two- and three-dimensional case.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, if one is interested in scattering length and effective range, then one has to use potentials that are not power-law potentials.

in two dimensions, a scattering length and effective range exist only if the potential is of finite range, while in three dimensions a scattering length always exists, but an effective range only if the potential has a sufficiently rapid decrease.

, in two and three dimensional S-wave scattering of central potentials, the low-energy expansion in powers of the momentum has an effective range and a scattering length if and only if the potential is of finite range and has a finite number of nodes in the radial wave function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the scattering length exists for any potential with an asymptotic behavior of the form of a power law, but the effective range exists only for a limited range of power-law potentials.
, if a potential is sufficiently short ranged, then the S-wave phase shifts are analytic functions of the momentum.

the effective range is a measure of the deviation from the asymptotic behavior of the phase-shift at low energies, and is therefore an indication of the range of the potential, whereas the scattering length is an indication of the strength of the potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scattering length and effective range are not always the only two parameters in the low-energy phase-shift expansion, but rather that higher-order corrections can appear.
in two dimensions there is no effective range, and in three dimensions there is no scattering length.
in the low-energy scattering regime the phase shift is determined by the behavior of the potential at short distances and not by the long-range tail of the potential.
